Mother bring her 18 month old girl, weight about 11.6 kg. She say the baby cry and pull off the breast after two minutes and she think her milk is not enough. Baby looks well, no fever, no cough. What can I do?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: BREAST FEEDING
---
Check the baby first for the causes in the manual: low birth weight, birth trauma, infection (chest, meningitis, urine), cleft lip or palate, trisomy 21. If any, treat or refer.
Check the mother too: her illness, cracked, flat or inverted nipples, or if she is an adopting mother who never lactated. Treat if you can, refer to the midwife or paediatric nurse.
Watch one full feed: is the baby sucking frequently and well, good positioning and attachment?
If the milk supply is really poor, the manual allows a trial of metoclopramide 10 mg tds or chlorpromazine 25 mg tds until the supply increases, and the mother should suckle often even if no milk comes at first.
Baby formula only if a doctor prescribes it.
Come back in 2 days if the baby is still not feeding well or is not passing urine.

[guideline: PAEDIATRIC PHARMACY ADVICE p14] GIVING MEDICINES TO CHILDREN Rectal medicines - Use of gloves is recommended when inserting a suppository - Position the child on their left side with the upper leg bent and buttocks separated - Moisten the suppository with lubricating jelly to help with insertion - Insert gently to about half the length of the finger o For a bullet shaped suppository, insert the pointy end first o For a tear-drop shaped suppository, insert the larger rounded end first - Hold the buttocks together for five minutes to stop the suppository being expelled - Have the child lie down or sit for about 10 minutes - Discourage the child from going to the toilet after the suppository has been given Eye medicines - Wash your hands - Clean the eyes with a clean, damp towel - Tilt head back - small children can lay on their back - Make sure the dropper does not touch the eyes or eyelashes - Pull down gently on lower eye lid - Drop the solution or squeeze 1.5cm of ointment into eyelid - Have the child close the eye for one minute - Apply pressure to the inner corner of the eye to stop the loss of medication through the duct - If giving more than one drop then wait five minutes in between drops to make sure everything gets absorbed Note: eye ointments can temporarily blur vision Ear medicines - Put child on their side - Straighten the ear canal o For infants the ear should be pulled back and down o For older children the ear should be pulled back and up. - The child should remain on their side for five minutes to allow the drops to enter the ear - Cotton wool can be used as a plug to prevent the drops from running out of the ear

assistant:

STM: NEWBORN BABIES - NEONATAL INFECTIONS
---
This newborn has fever, poor feeding and umbilical redness, all danger signs for serious neonatal infection.
Refer the baby on the next boat tomorrow morning to the AHC or hospital.
While waiting, keep the baby warm with skin-to-skin contact with the mother, cover both with a blanket.
Check blood sugar if you can; if low give expressed breast milk by cup or spoon every 2 hours.
Record the times of feeds, temperature and breathing, and send the note with them on the boat.

Poor feeding and cyanosis in a 3 day old baby are danger signs for serious infection.

assistant:

Before the boat: give artesunate 2.4 mg/kg intramuscularly (about 42 mg for 17.3 kg) if you have it and are trained.

Check blood sugar if you can and treat low sugar as the manual says.
Write down the fit time and the RDT result and send the note with her.
If she fits again on the way, protect her airway and tell the receiving nurse.

[guideline: FEVER p40] - Fever is defined as an axillary (under the arm) temperature greater than 37.5 oC - Fever in itself is not dangerous as it helps the body to fight infection CAUSES The common causes of fever in children are: - Common viral infections: upper respiratory tract infection, measles, gastroenteritis - Common bacterial: pneumonia, meningitis, otitis media, urinary tract infections - Other: Malaria, tuberculosis INVESTIGATIONS - Consider blood film or rapid diagnostic test for malaria parasites - If possible, collect and test a urine sample MANAGEMENT - Treat the cause of the fever - Consider antimalarials - Consider giving paracetamol if fever above 38ºC AND the child is irritable o Dose: 15mg/kg (max 1g) every 4 to 6 hours (maximum 4 doses in 24 hours) o Do not use aspirin in children for fever - Give extra fluids Consider the following causes for fever greater than 7 days: - Abscess - Salmonella infection - Infective endocarditis - Rheumatic fever - Tuberculosis Fever helps the body to fight infection Try to find and treat the cause of the fever

[guideline: BREAST FEEDING p26] PROMOTE BREAST FEEDING - It is safe, simple, readily available and cheap - It contains all the nutrients that the baby needs to grow - It reduces the risk of diarrhoea, pneumonia, malnutrition and other diseases - Helps encourage bonding between mother and baby FACTS ABOUT BREAST FEEDING - Breast feeding should begin within the first hour after delivery - The first yellow milk a mother makes (colostrum) should be given to the baby. o It should not be thrown away as it contains important immunoglobulins that are part of the baby's defense against infection - The easiest and best schedule is 'on-demand' breast feeding o Infants who cannot demand feed (such as low birth weight or sick babies) should be fed every 2-3 hours o Infants who cannot suck on the breast (eg. very premature babies) should be given expressed breast milk (EBM) by cup/spoon or by NG tube - Ideally all babies should be exclusively breast fed for the first 6 months o Solids should be introduced from 6 months o Cow's milk or powdered milk should be avoided before the age of 12 months because of the risk of iron-deficiency anaemia - Breast feeding should continue for as long as possible. - Breast feeding policies should be supported and upheld always - Bottles with teats and baby cups with spouts should discouraged. o They are difficult to sterilize and may result in infections such as diarrhoea - For facts about breast feeding in HIV positive mothers

Watch for danger signs: not feeding, lethargic, convulsions, fast breathing, fever under 2 months—refer now if any.

Pikinini blong mi 18 month, weight around 11.6 kg. Hem garem fever for more than 2 weeks finis and no improvement with the medicine we gave. Transport is next boat tomorrow morning. What should I prepare for transfer?
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NEXT_TRANSPORT
STM: ADVICE FOR TRANSFERING PATIENTS
---
Unexplained fever for more than 2 weeks with treatment is a reason to refer to hospital.
Give paracetamol 15 mg per kilo (about 174 mg) every 6 hours while waiting for the boat.
Give extra fluids by mouth and keep the child warm.
Write a referral letter: age, weight, how long the fever, what medicine was given, and no RDT or ACT here.
Send the child with the mother and the letter on the next boat.

user:

[guideline: NEWBORN BABIES LESS THAN 2.5 KG WEIGHT p66] Babies with low birth weight need special care. They are at risk of becoming cold (hypothermia), having low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia) and infection. Some babies are small because they are born prematurely (before they are due). Infection is an important cause of premature labour. MANAGEMENT - Keep the baby warm - Small babies get cold easily. o Keep the baby skin to skin when possible (together with mother or father) well wrapped up in a warm room. - Start feeds within 1 hour of delivery o Babies who can suck should be breastfed. o Babies who cannot be breastfed should be given expressed breast milk (EBM) by cup and spoon. Change to breastfeeding when the baby starts to suck well from the breast. o Use a NG tube for those less than 1.5kg, or not taking EBM well by cup and spoon or are sick. Nasogastric tubes should be changed twice a week. When the baby can suck well, change to breast feeding or cup and spoon o If EBM unavailable consider IV access and fluids, transfer to hospital
We have a newborn here in our village clinic, born last night, mother says baby is small and looks weak. Baby weighs 3.6 kg. I put baby skin to skin with mother but mother is tired now. What else must I do?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: NEWBORN BABIES LESS THAN 2.5 KG WEIGHT
---
This baby is 3.6 kg, which is above 2.5 kg, so this section does not fully match. Check the birth weight again and use EARLY ESSENTIAL NEWBORN CARE or standard newborn care if truly 3.6 kg.
If the weight is correct at 2.5 kg or less: keep baby skin to skin with father or another warm adult when mother rests, wrapped well in a warm room.
Start feeds within 1 hour of delivery; if baby can suck, breastfeed directly.
If baby cannot suck, give expressed breast milk by cup and spoon until sucking improves.
Check for danger signs: unable to feed, cold skin, fits, fast breathing, lethargy. Refer now if any appear.
Kambak tomoro fo check weight gain an feeding.

Diarrhoea for longer than 2 weeks that does not improve with appropriate treatment needs referral to hospital.
Since transport is next boat, start treatment while waiting: give oral rehydration solution (ORS) frequently and continue feeding.

Send with the next boat and tell the mother to keep giving fluids.

Girl 18 months, 12.1 kg. Fever and cough 3 days, no danger signs, drinking well. We have amoxycillin and paracetamol. How much paracetamol by weight?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: PAEDIATRIC DRUG DOSES
---
Paracetamol is 15 mg for every kilo, so for 12.1 kg give 180 mg each dose.
Give it every 4 to 6 hours, no more than 4 doses in 24 hours.
Only give it if the fever is above 38 C and the child is irritable.
Never give aspirin to a child.
Give extra water and keep feeding her.
Come back in 2 days, or at once if she cannot drink, vomits everything, has a convulsion or becomes very sleepy.

user:

[guideline: NEWBORN BABIES LESS THAN 2.5 KG WEIGHT p66] Babies with low birth weight need special care. They are at risk of becoming cold (hypothermia), having low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia) and infection. Some babies are small because they are born prematurely (before they are due). Infection is an important cause of premature labour. MANAGEMENT - Keep the baby warm - Small babies get cold easily. o Keep the baby skin to skin when possible (together with mother or father) well wrapped up in a warm room. - Start feeds within 1 hour of delivery o Babies who can suck should be breastfed. o Babies who cannot be breastfed should be given expressed breast milk (EBM) by cup and spoon. Change to breastfeeding when the baby starts to suck well from the breast. o Use a NG tube for those less than 1.5kg, or not taking EBM well by cup and spoon or are sick. Nasogastric tubes should be changed twice a week. When the baby can suck well, change to breast feeding or cup and spoon o If EBM unavailable consider IV access and fluids, transfer to hospital

Keep the baby skin to skin with you, well wrapped, in a warm room, day and night. Feed him within 1 hour and then at least every 2 to 3 hours; wake him to feed if he sleeps too long. If he cannot suck well, give expressed breast milk by cup and spoon. Bring him back at once if he feels cold, stops feeding, breathes fast, or becomes floppy. Come back tomorrow for a weight and feeding check.

The most common causes of neonatal death are: - Preterm birth complications - Birth asphyxia - Neonatal infections - Congenital abnormalities Early Essential Newborn Care (EENC) practices focus on improving the quality of care during labour, delivery and immediately after birth. Most newborns only require simple supportive care during and after delivery. All babies (including if born by caesarean, sick or preterm), benefit from: - Immediate thorough drying - Skin-to-skin contact - Early and exclusive breast-feeding - Cord clamping after pulsations stop (no earlier than 1 minute). BORN BEFORE ARRIVAL (BBA) Some babies are born at home or before being brought to the clinic or hospital. It is important to weigh the baby, as babies less than 2.5kg need special care. These babies may be at added risk of infection. MANAGEMENT FOR ALL BABIES - Leave baby with mother, support breastfeeding and keep skin-to-skin for 90 minutes (if baby is well) before other treatments below - Weigh and examine the baby o If the baby looks unwell or has fast breathing (>60/minute), give oxygen by nasal catheter and commence treatment for infection o If the baby weighs less than 2.5kg, see guideline for low birth weight babies - Vitamin K (phytomenadione) 1mg IM once o Use 1mg/1ml ampoule. Do NOT use 10mg/ml ampoule. - Hepatitis B and BCG vaccines o Best given at or soon after birth - Apply tetracycline eye ointment ...
Baby born on the way to the clinic this morning, mother says labour was quick. Baby is 1 month old, about 4.1 kg, baby is warm and crying, feeding ok. What do I do now for the cord and the first feed?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: EARLY ESSENTIAL NEWBORN CARE
---
Keep the baby skin-to-skin with mother and let her breastfeed within the first hour, exclusive breastfeeding only.
Dry the baby well, cover the head, and leave the cord dry and open, no medicine on it.
Weigh and examine the baby; at 4.1 kg this baby is above 2.5 kg so no special low birth weight care needed.
Give vitamin K 1 mg IM once using the 1 mg/1 ml ampoule, never the 10 mg/ml one.
Give BCG and hepatitis B vaccines now, and apply tetracycline eye ointment.
Come back at once if the baby stops feeding, breathes fast over 60 a minute, or feels cold or hot.

[guideline: FEVER p40] - Fever is defined as an axillary (under the arm) temperature greater than 37.5 oC - Fever in itself is not dangerous as it helps the body to fight infection CAUSES The common causes of fever in children are: - Common viral infections: upper respiratory tract infection, measles, gastroenteritis - Common bacterial: pneumonia, meningitis, otitis media, urinary tract infections - Other: Malaria, tuberculosis INVESTIGATIONS - Consider blood film or rapid diagnostic test for malaria parasites - If possible, collect and test a urine sample MANAGEMENT - Treat the cause of the fever - Consider antimalarials - Consider giving paracetamol if fever above 38ºC AND the child is irritable o Dose: 15mg/kg (max 1g) every 4 to 6 hours (maximum 4 doses in 24 hours) o Do not use aspirin in children for fever - Give extra fluids Consider the following causes for fever greater than 7 days: - Abscess - Salmonella infection - Infective endocarditis - Rheumatic fever - Tuberculosis Fever helps the body to fight infection Try to find and treat the cause of the fever

Can occur in immunised children but usually a more mild illness SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - Cough and runny nose for 1 week (1st stage) followed by spasmodic cough with 'whooping' sound. May also present as a non-specific persistant cough - Vomiting often following a coughing spasm - Apnoea or cyanosis during coughing spasms - Fever is uncommon - There may be no clinical signs on examination and children may appear well between coughing spasms COMPLICATIONS - Infants < 6 months are at greatest risk and are commonly infected by family members - Apnoea - Severe pneumonia - Encephalopathy INVESTIGATIONS - Generally a clinical diagnosis - If persistant cough or other suggestive symptoms (weight loss, night sweats) remember to assess TB exposure and consider investigations if risk factors - Blood count (may be associated with high lymphocyte count) MANAGEMENT MANAGEMENT NOTES:

[guideline: FEVER p40] - Fever is defined as an axillary (under the arm) temperature greater than 37.5 oC - Fever in itself is not dangerous as it helps the body to fight infection CAUSES The common causes of fever in children are: - Common viral infections: upper respiratory tract infection, measles, gastroenteritis - Common bacterial: pneumonia, meningitis, otitis media, urinary tract infections - Other: Malaria, tuberculosis INVESTIGATIONS - Consider blood film or rapid diagnostic test for malaria parasites - If possible, collect and test a urine sample MANAGEMENT - Treat the cause of the fever - Consider antimalarials - Consider giving paracetamol if fever above 38ºC AND the child is irritable o Dose: 15mg/kg (max 1g) every 4 to 6 hours (maximum 4 doses in 24 hours) o Do not use aspirin in children for fever - Give extra fluids Consider the following causes for fever greater than 7 days: - Abscess - Salmonella infection - Infective endocarditis - Rheumatic fever - Tuberculosis Fever helps the body to fight infection Try to find and treat the cause of the fever

Check the temperature under the arm and do a malaria RDT today.
If the fever is above 38 and the baby is irritable, give paracetamol 80 mg (15 mg/kg) by mouth every 4 to 6 hours, maximum 4 doses in 24 hours.

Offer extra breastfeeds and water between feeds.
Come back in 2 days, or at once if the baby cannot drink, vomits everything, fits, or becomes floppy.

[guideline: BREAST FEEDING p26] PROMOTE BREAST FEEDING - It is safe, simple, readily available and cheap - It contains all the nutrients that the baby needs to grow - It reduces the risk of diarrhoea, pneumonia, malnutrition and other diseases - Helps encourage bonding between mother and baby FACTS ABOUT BREAST FEEDING - Breast feeding should begin within the first hour after delivery - The first yellow milk a mother makes (colostrum) should be given to the baby. o It should not be thrown away as it contains important immunoglobulins that are part of the baby's defense against infection - The easiest and best schedule is 'on-demand' breast feeding o Infants who cannot demand feed (such as low birth weight or sick babies) should be fed every 2-3 hours o Infants who cannot suck on the breast (eg. very premature babies) should be given expressed breast milk (EBM) by cup/spoon or by NG tube - Ideally all babies should be exclusively breast fed for the first 6 months o Solids should be introduced from 6 months o Cow's milk or powdered milk should be avoided before the age of 12 months because of the risk of iron-deficiency anaemia - Breast feeding should continue for as long as possible. - Breast feeding policies should be supported and upheld always - Bottles with teats and baby cups with spouts should discouraged. o They are difficult to sterilize and may result in infections such as diarrhoea - For facts about breast feeding in HIV positive mothers

Because transport is none and the baby is under 2 months old, call the AHC or hospital by radio or phone now and ask them to review the baby.

Come back quickly if the baby stops feeding, breathes fast, or gets chest indrawing.

Tablets or capsules - Follow with water or a favourite drink - For young chidren, many tablets can be crushed on a clean spoon and mixed with a little water or juice - Some tablets should not be crushed or broken - check with your pharmacy officer or Medicines Information Centre (MIC) if you are not sure iii. Portion of a tablet or capsule - Try to round doses (where appropriate) to an easily measured dose e.g. ¼, ½, full tablet - If you cannot round the dose give the carers instructions and demonstrate how to get the correct dose - For a portion of a dose crush and disperse the tablet in 10 ml of water and give the correct portion. Use a new tablet each time. - To calculate the portion of mixture to give: (dose/tablet strength) x 10mL e.g. for a 40 mg dose of a 100 mg tablet: Crush and disperse the tablet in 10 mL of water in a syringe Shake well Discard 6 mL of the liquid and give the child the remaining 4 mL For all oral medicines: - Observe child to make sure medicine is not vomitted back up. - If the medicine is vomited within 30 minutes of taking, repeat the dose.

Tablets or capsules - Follow with water or a favourite drink - For young chidren, many tablets can be crushed on a clean spoon and mixed with a little water or juice - Some tablets should not be crushed or broken - check with your pharmacy officer or Medicines Information Centre (MIC) if you are not sure iii. Portion of a tablet or capsule - Try to round doses (where appropriate) to an easily measured dose e.g. ¼, ½, full tablet - If you cannot round the dose give the carers instructions and demonstrate how to get the correct dose - For a portion of a dose crush and disperse the tablet in 10 ml of water and give the correct portion. Use a new tablet each time. - To calculate the portion of mixture to give: (dose/tablet strength) x 10mL e.g. for a 40 mg dose of a 100 mg tablet: Crush and disperse the tablet in 10 mL of water in a syringe Shake well Discard 6 mL of the liquid and give the child the remaining 4 mL For all oral medicines: - Observe child to make sure medicine is not vomitted back up. - If the medicine is vomited within 30 minutes of taking, repeat the dose.

assistant:

If he stops breathing or turns blue, start resuscitation and get help at once.

[guideline: FEVER p40] - Fever is defined as an axillary (under the arm) temperature greater than 37.5 oC - Fever in itself is not dangerous as it helps the body to fight infection CAUSES The common causes of fever in children are: - Common viral infections: upper respiratory tract infection, measles, gastroenteritis - Common bacterial: pneumonia, meningitis, otitis media, urinary tract infections - Other: Malaria, tuberculosis INVESTIGATIONS - Consider blood film or rapid diagnostic test for malaria parasites - If possible, collect and test a urine sample MANAGEMENT - Treat the cause of the fever - Consider antimalarials - Consider giving paracetamol if fever above 38ºC AND the child is irritable o Dose: 15mg/kg (max 1g) every 4 to 6 hours (maximum 4 doses in 24 hours) o Do not use aspirin in children for fever - Give extra fluids Consider the following causes for fever greater than 7 days: - Abscess - Salmonella infection - Infective endocarditis - Rheumatic fever - Tuberculosis Fever helps the body to fight infection Try to find and treat the cause of the fever
I have a 3 and a half year old girl, around 14 kg. She has had fever for 9 days now. It goes up and down. She is eating a little bit and drinking water. No rash, no cough. The truck is here now if we need to go. What should I do?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: FEVER
---
Fever more than 7 days needs careful look for abscess, typhoid, TB or rheumatic fever.
Check her whole body for abscess, listen to heart for murmur, look at joints for swelling.
Do malaria RDT if you can. Collect urine if possible.
Paracetamol 210 mg (15 mg per kg) every 4 to 6 hours if fever above 38 and she is irritable. Maximum 4 doses in 24 hours.
Give extra fluids. Come back tomorrow or sooner if worse.
Watch for danger signs: cannot drink, vomits everything, convulsion, very sleepy, stiff neck, fast breathing with chest indrawing.

It is important to closely monitor the baby (weigh baby daily) as it is easy to give them too much. [guideline: FEVER p40] - Fever is defined as an axillary (under the arm) temperature greater than 37.5 oC - Fever in itself is not dangerous as it helps the body to fight infection CAUSES The common causes of fever in children are: - Common viral infections: upper respiratory tract infection, measles, gastroenteritis - Common bacterial: pneumonia, meningitis, otitis media, urinary tract infections - Other: Malaria, tuberculosis INVESTIGATIONS - Consider blood film or rapid diagnostic test for malaria parasites - If possible, collect and test a urine sample MANAGEMENT - Treat the cause of the fever - Consider antimalarials - Consider giving paracetamol if fever above 38ºC AND the child is irritable o Dose: 15mg/kg (max 1g) every 4 to 6 hours (maximum 4 doses in 24 hours) o Do not use aspirin in children for fever - Give extra fluids Consider the following causes for fever greater than 7 days: - Abscess - Salmonella infection - Infective endocarditis - Rheumatic fever - Tuberculosis Fever helps the body to fight infection Try to find and treat the cause of the fever
Boy 4 yia, 17.3 kilo, hot bodi 2 day an hem no laek kaikai tumas, bat hem dring gud an no toroaot. RDT i stap, mi testim hem. No ACT long klinik. Next boat i kam tumoro. Wanem mi givim?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: FEVER
---
No danger sign now, so manage the fever at the clinic and wait for the RDT result.
Give paracetamol 260 mg (15 mg per kg for 17.3 kg) every 4 to 6 hours, max 4 doses in 24 hours.
Do not give aspirin. Give extra fluids and encourage food.
If the RDT is positive and no ACT is in stock, ask the AHC by radio for antimalarial treatment and plan the next boat.
Check ears, throat, chest and urine for other causes.
Come back in 2 days, or sooner if he stops drinking, vomits everything, fits, or has stiff neck.

[guideline: MENINGITIS p62] Meningitis is a very severe infection of the coverings of the brain (meninges) CAUSES - Bacteria (e.g: Meningoccous, Pneumococcus, Haemophilus, E.Coli) - Malaria (meningitis can be a complication cerebral malaria) - Viruses (e.g: enterovirus, HSV, VZ) - Tuberculosis - Fungus (e.g. cryptococcus) SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - Fever, headache, irritability, lethergy - Poor feeding, vomiting or diarrhoea - Bulging fontanelle (infants) - Photophobia, neck stiffness (older children) - Convulsions, decreased concious state
Boy 5 years, about 16.8 kg. Fever since yesterday and now the neck is stiff, he does not want the light in his eyes and he is drowsy, hard to wake. No boat until tomorrow morning. What do I do while we wait?
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NEXT_TRANSPORT
STM: MENINGITIS
---
Stiff neck with drowsy and fever is a danger sign, so this child must go to hospital on the next boat.
Keep him lying still, in the shade, away from bright light, and watch his breathing.
If he can swallow, give the first dose of the antibiotic you stock now, and write the time on the referral note.
If he cannot swallow or he fits, keep the airway open and do not force anything by mouth.
Send the mother with the note, and radio the AHC now to say the child is coming tomorrow.

[guideline: BREAST FEEDING p26] DIFFICULTY BREAST FEEDING - Check the baby for underlying causes and treat: o Premature or low birth weight o Birth trauma o Infections (especially respiratory, meningitis, urinary tract infection) o Congenital problems such as cleft lip/ palate (feed with cup & spoon, refer to hospital) and trisomy 21 - Check the mother for any underlying problems (treat if possible, refer to midwife, paediatric nurse, paediatrician or obstetrician) o Maternal illness o Breast problem (cracked, flat or inverted nipples) o Adopting mother, never previously lactated - Problems with 'inadequate' milk supply o Check baby is sucking frequently and well (check positioning/ attachment) o Check to see if breast milk supply is really inadequate. If poor milk supply: - Consider giving the mother a trial of metoclopramide 10 mg tds OR chlorpromazine 25mg tds (until the breast milk supply increases) - Encourage mother to suckle the baby frequently, even if there is no breast milk to begin with o Baby formula should only be used if prescribed by a doctor

[guideline: EARLY ESSENTIAL NEWBORN CARE p64] Newborn deaths are concentrated towards the first three days of life, especially the first 24 hours. The most common causes of neonatal death are: - Preterm birth complications - Birth asphyxia - Neonatal infections - Congenital abnormalities Early Essential Newborn Care (EENC) practices focus on improving the quality of care during labour, delivery and immediately after birth. Most newborns only require simple supportive care during and after delivery. All babies (including if born by caesarean, sick or preterm), benefit from: - Immediate thorough drying - Skin-to-skin contact - Early and exclusive breast-feeding - Cord clamping after pulsations stop (no earlier than 1 minute). BORN BEFORE ARRIVAL (BBA) Some babies are born at home or before being brought to the clinic or hospital. It is important to weigh the baby, as babies less than 2.5kg need special care. These babies may be at added risk of infection. MANAGEMENT FOR ALL BABIES - Leave baby with mother, support breastfeeding and keep skin-to-skin for 90 minutes (if baby is well) before other treatments below - Weigh and examine the baby o If the baby looks unwell or has fast breathing (>60/minute), give oxygen by nasal catheter and commence treatment for infection o If the baby weighs less than 2.5kg, see guideline for low birth weight babies - Vitamin K (phytomenadione) 1mg IM once o Use 1mg/1ml ampoule. [guideline: PERTUSSIS (WHOOPING COUGH) p81] Whooping cough occurs when the bacteria Bordetella pertussis gets into the respiratory tract and causes a bloody mucous to be formed CAUSE - Spread by air droplets - Patients are contagious for 21 days after the onset of the cough, if untreated - Non-vaccinated children most commonly affected. Can occur in immunised children but usually a more mild illness SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - Cough and runny nose for 1 week (1st stage) followed by spasmodic cough with 'whooping' sound. May also present as a non-specific persistant cough - Vomiting often following a coughing spasm - Apnoea or cyanosis during coughing spasms - Fever is uncommon - There may be no clinical signs on examination and children may appear well between coughing spasms COMPLICATIONS - Infants < 6 months are at greatest risk and are commonly infected by family members - Apnoea - Severe pneumonia - Encephalopathy INVESTIGATIONS - Generally a clinical diagnosis - If persistant cough or other suggestive symptoms (weight loss, night sweats) remember to assess TB exposure and consider investigations if risk factors - Blood count (may be associated with high lymphocyte count) MANAGEMENT MANAGEMENT NOTES:
Bebi 8 manis, 8.9 kilo, hem garem kof wea strong tumas an mekem whoop saon, afta hem toraot. Sometaim hem go blu long fes taem hem kof. Hem no garem hot bodi. Mama se neba tekem olketa injection yet. Bot i kam long Mande. Wanem mi mas duim nao?

Give 3rd dose 2-4 weeks later if eye signs suggestive of Vit A deficiency Immunise contacts Give measles vaccine to all siblings aged 6 months-5 years if not fully vaccinated If unclear vaccination history ...
5 year old boy, 19.4 kg, fever 3 days now rash starting on face and spreading down. Red eyes, runny nose, bad cough, sore mouth. Mum says no measles vaccine. No RDT at clinic but we have ACT. No transport today, village is longwe. What to give?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: MEASLES
---
This is measles: red rash from head down, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, fever. No danger signs so manage here.
Give vitamin A 200,000 Units today and tomorrow, then a 3rd dose in 2-4 weeks because of red eyes.
Check for complications: fast breathing, chest indrawing, diarrhoea, dehydration, stridor. Admit if any present.
Give measles vaccine to all siblings 6 months to 5 years if not vaccinated.
Keep him away from other children. Paracetamol for fever. Come back tomorrow if rash worsens or new symptoms.
Ask mum about eye problems at night or Bitot spots.

assistant:

STM: ASTHMA

Before she goes give Magnesium Sulfate 50% 2.2 ml IV (0.1 ml/kg = 50 mg/kg) over 20 minutes if you can start a line.

[guideline: NEWBORN BABIES LESS THAN 2.5 KG WEIGHT p66] Babies with low birth weight need special care. They are at risk of becoming cold (hypothermia), having low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia) and infection. Some babies are small because they are born prematurely (before they are due). Infection is an important cause of premature labour. MANAGEMENT - Keep the baby warm - Small babies get cold easily. o Keep the baby skin to skin when possible (together with mother or father) well wrapped up in a warm room. - Start feeds within 1 hour of delivery o Babies who can suck should be breastfed. o Babies who cannot be breastfed should be given expressed breast milk (EBM) by cup and spoon. Change to breastfeeding when the baby starts to suck well from the breast. o Use a NG tube for those less than 1.5kg, or not taking EBM well by cup and spoon or are sick. Nasogastric tubes should be changed twice a week. When the baby can suck well, change to breast feeding or cup and spoon o If EBM unavailable consider IV access and fluids, transfer to hospital

Kambak kwiktaem sapos hem kol tumas, no laek susu, toraot, o hem les an no muvum bodi. Kambak long klinik long 2 dei.

[guideline: BREAST FEEDING p26] PROMOTE BREAST FEEDING - It is safe, simple, readily available and cheap - It contains all the nutrients that the baby needs to grow - It reduces the risk of diarrhoea, pneumonia, malnutrition and other diseases - Helps encourage bonding between mother and baby FACTS ABOUT BREAST FEEDING - Breast feeding should begin within the first hour after delivery - The first yellow milk a mother makes (colostrum) should be given to the baby. o It should not be thrown away as it contains important immunoglobulins that are part of the baby's defense against infection - The easiest and best schedule is 'on-demand' breast feeding o Infants who cannot demand feed (such as low birth weight or sick babies) should be fed every 2-3 hours o Infants who cannot suck on the breast (eg. very premature babies) should be given expressed breast milk (EBM) by cup/spoon or by NG tube - Ideally all babies should be exclusively breast fed for the first 6 months o Solids should be introduced from 6 months o Cow's milk or powdered milk should be avoided before the age of 12 months because of the risk of iron-deficiency anaemia - Breast feeding should continue for as long as possible. - Breast feeding policies should be supported and upheld always - Bottles with teats and baby cups with spouts should discouraged. o They are difficult to sterilize and may result in infections such as diarrhoea - For facts about breast feeding in HIV positive mothers

---

Sapos bebi no fit dring, toraot evri samting, o slip tumas, kolem mi o dokta long fon o radio kwiktaem. Lukluk fo saen blong denja.

Witnessing resuscitation, although traumatic, often assists in the families understanding and acceptance ...

The most common causes of neonatal death are: - Preterm birth complications - Birth asphyxia - Neonatal infections - Congenital abnormalities Early Essential Newborn Care (EENC) practices focus on improving the quality of care during labour, delivery and immediately after birth. Most newborns only require simple supportive care during and after delivery. All babies (including if born by caesarean, sick or preterm), benefit from: - Immediate thorough drying - Skin-to-skin contact - Early and exclusive breast-feeding - Cord clamping after pulsations stop (no earlier than 1 minute). [guideline: MEASLES p61] - Measles is a viral infection which causes a red, raised rash - It is transmitted by droplets produced by sneezing and coughing - The incubation period is between 7 and 21 days - Measles is very infectious from 7 days before until 2 days after the rash appears SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - Fever (before the rash appears) - Blotchy red rash, starting on head/neck moving down over the body (day 3-7) - Look for the 3 C's: Cough, Coryza (runny nose), Conjunctivitis - Sore mouth - Koplick spots (may have small white spots in mouth) - Diarrhoea PREVENTION - Immunisation - Avoiding contact with others who are infected MANAGEMENT Admission/OutpatientsMost can be managed as Outpatients Admit if complications: pneumonia, diarrhoea, dehydration, stridor Admit children with underlying cardiac disease/respiratory disease Admit if immunocompromised Malnutrition Consider nutritional status and SAM management Treat co-existing infection Oral thrush, conjunctivitis, pneumonia or diarrhoea Refer to relevant section in STM for treatment advice Consider malaria Consider investigation and treatment if from high risk area Give Vitamin A <6 months: 50,000 Units, 6 months - 1 year: 100,000 Units, >1 year: 200,000 Units Daily for 2 days. Give 3rd dose 2-4 weeks later if eye signs suggestive of Vit A deficiency Immunise contacts Give measles vaccine to all siblings aged 6 months-5 years if not fully vaccinated If unclear vaccination history ...

[guideline: DIARRHOEA p36] HOME MANAGEMENT - Give the child more fluids more often. Any locally available home fluid should be used e.g: thin soups from boiled vegetables (rice water, sweet potato water, banana water), green coconut water or cooled boiled water - Give child as much fluid as they will drink and after every watery stool - Continue giving the extra fluids until the diarrhoea stops - Give the child plenty of food to prevent undernutrition - Continue to breast feed frequently. - Give fresh fruit or mashed banana to provide potassium. - Give freshly prepared foods. Rice, sweet potato or taro mixed with vegetable and meat or fish are good. Cook and mash or grind food well - Encourage the child to eat; offer food at least 6 times a day - After the diarrhoea stops, give an extra meal each day for two weeks - Ask the mother to bring the child back for review if - Many watery stools or repeated vomitting - Very thirsty or inadequately drinking or eating - Fever and unwell - Blood in the stool - Symptom's persist greater than 2 weeks - Counsel family that due to inflammation of the gut, loose bowel motions may continue for up to 2 weeks however the diarrhoea should slowly improve. - If persistant, see prolonged diarrhoea (>14 days)
I am at the rural clinic in Marau. Mother brought her 3 year old boy with watery stools since yesterday. He is alert and drinking well, eyes look normal, no vomiting. Weight 13.8 kg. What should I tell her?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: DIARRHOEA
---
Tell the mother to give extra fluids after every watery stool: rice water, sweet potato water, green coconut water, or cooled boiled water.
Continue breastfeeding often and give food at least 6 times a day: mashed rice, taro, vegetables, meat or fish.
Give fresh fruit or mashed banana for potassium.
Bring him back if he has many watery stools, repeated vomiting, gets very thirsty, has fever, blood in stool, or if this lasts more than 2 weeks.
Loose stools may continue up to 2 weeks but should slowly improve.

assistant:

STM: DIARRHOEA

This young infant needs close watching even though he looks well now.
Give extra breast milk after every watery stool and ensure mother feeds frequently.
If not breastfed, give cooled boiled water or green coconut water between feeds.
Watch very carefully for danger signs: repeated vomiting, very thirsty, fever, blood in stool, many watery stools, or if he becomes lethargic.
Bring him back at once if any danger sign appears, or if diarrhoea persists beyond 2 weeks.
Return tomorrow for review even if he seems well.

[guideline: PERTUSSIS (WHOOPING COUGH) p81] Whooping cough occurs when the bacteria Bordetella pertussis gets into the respiratory tract and causes a bloody mucous to be formed CAUSE - Spread by air droplets - Patients are contagious for 21 days after the onset of the cough, if untreated - Non-vaccinated children most commonly affected. Can occur in immunised children but usually a more mild illness SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - Cough and runny nose for 1 week (1st stage) followed by spasmodic cough with 'whooping' sound. May also present as a non-specific persistant cough - Vomiting often following a coughing spasm - Apnoea or cyanosis during coughing spasms - Fever is uncommon - There may be no clinical signs on examination and children may appear well between coughing spasms COMPLICATIONS - Infants < 6 months are at greatest risk and are commonly infected by family members - Apnoea - Severe pneumonia - Encephalopathy INVESTIGATIONS - Generally a clinical diagnosis - If persistant cough or other suggestive symptoms (weight loss, night sweats) remember to assess TB exposure and consider investigations if risk factors - Blood count (may be associated with high lymphocyte count) MANAGEMENT MANAGEMENT NOTES:

May also present as a non-specific persistant cough - Vomiting often following a coughing spasm - Apnoea or cyanosis during coughing spasms - Fever is uncommon - There may be no clinical signs on examination and children may appear well between coughing spasms COMPLICATIONS - Infants < 6 months are at greatest risk and are commonly infected by family members - Apnoea - Severe pneumonia - Encephalopathy INVESTIGATIONS - Generally a clinical diagnosis - If persistant cough or other suggestive symptoms (weight loss, night sweats) remember to assess TB exposure and consider investigations if risk factors - Blood count (may be associated with high lymphocyte count) MANAGEMENT MANAGEMENT NOTES:

Check MPS or RDT - Note the type of malaria (thin film) and the parasite count (thick film) - A single negative film or antigen does not exclude malaria - If strong suspicion, thick and thin films should be repeated with fever spikes until positive test or 3 negatives obtained - RDT can remain positive for up to 6 weeks after malaria has been treated - Always think about other infections, even if the MPS or RDT is positive - A child with fever and decreased conciousness might have meningitis - Classify as uncomplicated versus complicated and manage accordingly If you cannot test for malaria, treat presumptively Very sick children should be treated for severe malaria

[guideline: MALARIA p53] INVESTIGATION - Malaria slide (MPS) OR Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) - Blood glucose MANAGEMENT - Consider malaria in any child with a fever. Check MPS or RDT - Note the type of malaria (thin film) and the parasite count (thick film) - A single negative film or antigen does not exclude malaria - If strong suspicion, thick and thin films should be repeated with fever spikes until positive test or 3 negatives obtained - RDT can remain positive for up to 6 weeks after malaria has been treated - Always think about other infections, even if the MPS or RDT is positive - A child with fever and decreased conciousness might have meningitis - Classify as uncomplicated versus complicated and manage accordingly If you cannot test for malaria, treat presumptively Very sick children should be treated for severe malaria

[guideline: BURNS AND SCALDS p27] CAUSES - A burn is usually caused by a hot object coming into contact with the skin - Chemicals such as acid can also cause burns - Hot liquids like boiling water often cause partial thickness burns or scalds MANAGEMENT MANAGEMENT GOAL NOTES First aid Immediately immerse burn in cold running water for 20 mins This is to reduce serverity, still of use up to 3 hours after the burn Do not place ice directly on the burn Irrigate chemical burns with large volumes of cool clean water Assess burn area Using the picture diagram above Burns < 10% : Give extra fluid by mouth (e.g. water, coconut, ORS) Burns > 10%: Refer to hospital urgently as they require IV fluids Look for stridor Or hoarse voice - this indicates upper airway inflammation Risk particularly in neck/facial burns Give pain relief Regular paracetamol and consider morphine (0.1mg/kg per bolus) Clean & dress burn Clean and debride away dirt or dead tissue with antiseptic solution/salt water Apply silver sulphadiazine (SSD) cream or any antiseptic cream daily Fluids - 1st Day: Give an extra 4ml/kg for every 1% of area burnt PLUS maintenance fluids 1/2 of this extra fluid is given over 8 hours & remaining 1/2 over the next 16 hours Fluids - 2nd Day Give 3/4 of the total fluids required in the first day Give antibiotics If the burn looks infected Cloxacillin IV/oral depending on severity Monitor for sepsis Consider tetanus First check tetanus status Give if not fully immunised, >5 yrs since last tetanus or uncertain history ...
Baby 12 months, around 9.1 kg, pulled the kettle and boiling water splashed on the face and right hand yesterday. The skin is red and peeling, no fits, baby is breastfeeding and drinking fine. What should I do here at the clinic?
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NEXT_TRANSPORT
STM: BURNS AND SCALDS
---
This is a burn to the face and hand, so the child must go to hospital on the next boat.
First aid now: hold the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes, do not put ice on it.
Check for stridor or a hoarse voice. If either is there, go by radio to the AHC and send the child now.
Pain relief: paracetamol 15 mg/kg = 137 mg by mouth every 6 hours while waiting.
Keep giving extra fluids by mouth: water, coconut or ORS, and continue breastfeeding.
Cover the burn with a clean cloth and keep the child warm for the trip.

Boy 8 years old, 27.4 kg. He was playing with a lamp and his shirt caught fire. Burns on the chest and belly, I think more than 10 percent. He is awake, breathing fast, no stridor, no hoarse voice. Transport is available now.
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NOW
STM: BURNS AND SCALDS
---
Burns over more than 10 percent need IV fluids, so send this child to hospital now.
Give pain relief before the trip: paracetamol 15 mg/kg = 411 mg by mouth now, and morphine 0.1 mg/kg = 2.7 mg per bolus if you have it.
Start extra fluids by mouth while waiting: 4 ml/kg for every 1 percent burnt, plus maintenance.
Cover the burn with a clean dry cloth, do not put ice on it.
Check tetanus status and give tetanus if not fully immunised.
Watch for stridor or hoarse voice and tell the doctor at once if it comes.

18-month-old boy, weight 11.5 kg, brought by his grandmother. Bad ear pain, crying lots. Clinic has ampicillin vials. How much do I draw up for IM injection? RDT available but not done yet. Boat leaves this afternoon.
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: PAEDIATRIC DRUG DOSES
---
For ampicillin IM: reconstitute 500 mg vial with 1.7 mL WFI to get 250 mg/mL final concentration.
Dose is 50 mg/kg IM every 6 hours for moderate infections. For 11.5 kg that is 575 mg.
Draw up 2.3 mL of the 250 mg/mL solution to give 575 mg.
Inject deep into a large muscle immediately after drawing up. Use a fresh vial each time.
Send on this afternoon's boat if no improvement after 24 hours, or sooner if fever persists or child becomes lethargic.

Baby girl 8 months, 8.2 kg, high fever since yesterday. Village health worker did RDT, it was negative. We have artesunate vials at the clinic. Should I give it? How much? Next boat is in 2 days.
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NEXT_TRANSPORT
STM: FEVER
---
Negative RDT means malaria is unlikely, but fever in an 8-month-old needs careful assessment.
The artesunate dose shown is for severe malaria IV: 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 hours. For 8.2 kg that would be about 20 mg.
However, artesunate is only for severe malaria or when oral ACT cannot be taken. Do not give it for simple fever with negative RDT.
Give paracetamol 15 mg per kg (about 120 mg) for fever comfort, keep breastfeeding, and check for danger signs: lethargy, convulsions, stiff neck, unable to drink, vomits everything.
Send on next boat if any danger sign appears, or if fever lasts more than 2 days. Ask the nurse in charge to review before boat departs.

3-month-old baby, 5.5 kg, mother says he is not feeding well and feels hot. We have ampicillin here. Can I give it? How much to draw? Boat comes tomorrow. I am worried.
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NEXT_TRANSPORT
STM: PAEDIATRIC DRUG DOSES
---
Age under 2 months with fever is a danger sign, but this baby is 3 months so not automatic referral. Still, poor feeding and fever in a young infant is serious.
For ampicillin IM: 500 mg vial plus 1.7 mL WFI makes 250 mg/mL. Dose 50 mg/kg every 6 hours means 275 mg for 5.5 kg.
Draw up 1.1 mL of 250 mg/mL solution. Inject deep into large muscle immediately.
Also give first dose now before boat tomorrow, and write exact times on referral note. Keep baby warm, offer breast milk frequently.
Send on tomorrow's boat to hospital for full assessment. Call ahead by radio if possible.

Big boy 12 years old, 40 kg, from remote village. Cut his foot badly, looks infected, red swelling up the leg. We have ampicillin vials. How much for IV? RDT done, no malaria. Boat not until day after tomorrow.
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NEXT_TRANSPORT
STM: PAEDIATRIC DRUG DOSES
---
For ampicillin IV: 500 mg vial plus 4.7 mL WFI makes 100 mg/mL. Dose 50 mg/kg every 6 hours means 2000 mg for 40 kg.
For 2000 mg dose: draw 20 mL of 100 mg/mL. This exceeds 500 mg so dilute to 30 mg/mL with normal saline and infuse over 30 minutes.
Give first dose now. Draw up and use immediately. Write time and dose on referral note.
Red streaking up leg suggests serious infection. Send on next boat even if swelling improves.
Elevate leg, keep clean and dry. Give paracetamol for pain. Call hospital by radio to warn them.

---
The fit, the sleepiness and the pallor with jaundice are danger signs. He must go to hospital now, today.
No boat and no radio: send someone to the AHC or village radio to call the hospital and say a very sick child is coming.
While you wait, keep him on the side, keep him warm, and check blood sugar if you can.
If he fits again, protect the airway, note the time, and follow the CONVULSIONS section for diazepam if you are trained.
If you have artemether-lumefantrine, give the first dose for 17.5 kg as written in the manual before he travels.
Write the note: age, weight, fit time, how sleepy he is, and any drug given.

14-month-old girl, 11.6 kg, cough since yesterday, now breathing fast with chest indrawing and grunting, she took some breast milk this morning but not much since. Boat leaves tomorrow morning. What shall I do?
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NEXT_TRANSPORT
STM: PNEUMONIA
---
This is severe pneumonia: chest indrawing, grunting and poor feeding are danger signs. She must go to hospital on tomorrow's boat.
While waiting, give ampicillin 580 mg IM (50 mg/kg) now, and again every 6 hours until she boards.
Also give gentamicin 87 mg IM (7.5 mg/kg) once daily.
Keep her warm, give oxygen if you have it, and keep offering small breastfeeds.
Write referral note with age, weight, signs, drugs and times. Call AHC by radio to say she is coming.

STM: COLDS/ URTI
---
Colds hem viral, no antibiotic nidim. Hem dring gud an no danger signs, reassure mama.
RDT positive: consider antimalarials per guideline, so check FEVER/MALARIA fo ACT dose fo 6.9 kilo.
Givim paracetamol 103.5 mg (15 mg fo evri kilo) evri 4-6 aoa sapos hot bodi o pain.

[guideline: ASTHMA p21] - Asthma is caused by reversible tightening (bronchospasm) and inflammation in the airways - Children with asthma usually have recurrent episodes of wheeze and cough that improves with salbutamol - Think about asthma in any child older than 1 year who has shortness of breath, cough and wheeze. SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - The most important signs of severity are general appearance/mental state and increased work of breathing. Wheeze is a poor predictor of severity. - Rapid breathing ("short wind"), tachycardia, difficulty talking - Chest tightness, prolonged expiratory phase - Improvement in symptoms with salbutamol - Cough may be only at night or during activity - Low oxygen saturations may be a late sign - A silent chest is a pre-terminal sign
2 year old girl, around 11.6 kg. She wheezing bad since last night, now she cannot talk properly, chest very tight, silent when I listen with stethoscope. The health centre truck is here now and driver waiting.
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NOW
STM: ASTHMA
---
Silent chest is a pre-terminal sign. This is life-threatening asthma.
Give salbutamol nebuliser 2.5 mg or 6 puffs via spacer with mask now, repeat every 20 minutes while waiting.
Give oxygen 2-4 litres by nasal prongs if you have it, keep her sitting up.
Put her in the truck straight away with mother, continue salbutamol and oxygen if available during the trip.
Call the hospital or AHC by phone or radio now: say silent chest, unable to talk, severe asthma, age 2 years, weight 11.6 kg, salbutamol given and times.
Write referral note: silent chest, unable to speak, wheeze absent, salbutamol doses and times, oxygen started.

[guideline: DIARRHOEA p36] NOTES FLUID MANAGEMENT - If an IV can't be placed, insert an NG tube or intraosseous. The most common causes of neonatal death are: - Preterm birth complications - Birth asphyxia - Neonatal infections - Congenital abnormalities Early Essential Newborn Care (EENC) practices focus on improving the quality of care during labour, delivery and immediately after birth. Most newborns only require simple supportive care during and after delivery. All babies (including if born by caesarean, sick or preterm), benefit from: - Immediate thorough drying - Skin-to-skin contact - Early and exclusive breast-feeding - Cord clamping after pulsations stop (no earlier than 1 minute). BORN BEFORE ARRIVAL (BBA) Some babies are born at home or before being brought to the clinic or hospital. It is important to weigh the baby, as babies less than 2.5kg need special care. These babies may be at added risk of infection. MANAGEMENT FOR ALL BABIES - Leave baby with mother, support breastfeeding and keep skin-to-skin for 90 minutes (if baby is well) before other treatments below - Weigh and examine the baby o If the baby looks unwell or has fast breathing (>60/minute), give oxygen by nasal catheter and commence treatment for infection o If the baby weighs less than 2.5kg, see guideline for low birth weight babies - Vitamin K (phytomenadione) 1mg IM once o Use 1mg/1ml ampoule. Do NOT use 10mg/ml ampoule. - Hepatitis B and BCG vaccines o Best given at or soon after birth - Apply tetracycline eye ointment ...

Baby 1 year old, 9.0 kg, bad diarrhoea with blood, belly pain since yesterday. No RDT, no ACT here. Next boat come Tuesday morning. I want start ceftriaxone IM now for dysentery, I have 500 mg vial and 0.5% lignocaine. How I mix this one?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: PAEDIATRIC DRUG DOSES
---
Use 500 mg vial ceftriaxone. Put 1.3 mL lignocaine 0.5%, total 1.5 mL. This makes 330 mg/mL.
Inject deep into gluteal muscle. Do not put more than 1 g into each buttock.
0.5% lignocaine is less painful than 1% for IM injection.
This page shows dilution only. Radio AHC for correct ceftriaxone dose for 9.0 kg before you inject.
Also start oral rehydration now. Send on Tuesday boat if not better, or call emergency if blood more, belly very swollen, or child no drink.

Boy 6 year old, 20.6 kg, fell from coconut tree, deep cut on leg need stitch. We have ACT tablet but no RDT test. Next boat Friday morning to hospital. Doctor on radio say give lignocaine for local anaesthetic before I clean and stitch. I have 1 g vial, how I dilute for injection?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: PAEDIATRIC DRUG DOSES
---
Use 1 g vial lignocaine. Put 2.6 mL lignocaine, total 3 mL. This makes 330 mg/mL.

Give supplemental fluids via NGT / IV if poor feeding/vomiting Oral antibiotics: Children can usually be managed as an outpatient - Trimethoprim 4mg/kg orally every 12 hours (max 150mg) for 5 days OR if unavailable - Co-trimoxazole 4mg/kg orally every 12 hours for 5 days IV antibiotics needed if: (any one of the following) o Young children (< 3 months) o Systemically unwell (fevers and / or very sick) o Not feeding well or dehydrated o Not tolerating oral medicines o Failed oral therapy Give: - Ampicillin 50mg/kg (max 2g) IV / IM every 6 hours AND - Gentamicin IV once daily o Neonate < 34 weeks post conception 3mg/kg o Neonate > 34 weeks post conception 5mg/kg o Infant (over 1 month) and child < 10 years 7.5mg/kg (max 360mg) o Child > 10 years 6mg/kg (max 560mg) Check urine culture and adjust antibiotics according to sensitivities - Children with persistent haematuria, proteinuria or oedema should be referred to a paediatrician. These children might have kidney problems such as glomerulonephritis or nephrotic syndrome Antibiotic prophylaxis may be required in children with severe, recurrent UTIs. This should be discussed with a paediatrician.

[guideline: URINARY TRACT INFECTION p108] MANAGEMENT - Encourage breast-feeding/drinking. Give supplemental fluids via NGT / IV if poor feeding/vomiting Oral antibiotics: Children can usually be managed as an outpatient - Trimethoprim 4mg/kg orally every 12 hours (max 150mg) for 5 days OR if unavailable - Co-trimoxazole 4mg/kg orally every 12 hours for 5 days IV antibiotics needed if: (any one of the following) o Young children (< 3 months) o Systemically unwell (fevers and / or very sick) o Not feeding well or dehydrated o Not tolerating oral medicines o Failed oral therapy Give: - Ampicillin 50mg/kg (max 2g) IV / IM every 6 hours AND - Gentamicin IV once daily o Neonate < 34 weeks post conception 3mg/kg o Neonate > 34 weeks post conception 5mg/kg o Infant (over 1 month) and child < 10 years 7.5mg/kg (max 360mg) o Child > 10 years 6mg/kg (max 560mg) Check urine culture and adjust antibiotics according to sensitivities - Children with persistent haematuria, proteinuria or oedema should be referred to a paediatrician. These children might have kidney problems such as glomerulonephritis or nephrotic syndrome Antibiotic prophylaxis may be required in children with severe, recurrent UTIs. This should be discussed with a paediatrician.

assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: URINARY TRACT INFECTION
---
Givim Trimethoprim 32.8 mg evri 12 aoa fo 5 dei (4 mg fo evri kilo).
O sapos no gat, givim Co-trimoxazole 32.8 mg evri 12 aoa fo 5 dei.
Givim plante wata o susu, encourage mama fo mekem hem dring plante.
Lukluk sapos hem kaikai gud, no dehydrated, an hem tolerate oral meresin.
Kambak long 2 dei, o kwiktaem sapos hem kamap hot moa, no dring, o toraot evri samting.

The 7 year old boy at our clinic has had pus coming out of his right ear for nearly three weeks now. He is eating and playing, no fever, no fitting. His mother says she cleans it with a cloth. What should I do?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: OTITIS MEDIA - ACUTE & CHRONIC
---
Pus from the ear for more than 2 weeks is chronic otitis media.
Do ear toileting 3 times every day, and keep the ear dry.
Put chloramphenicol or ciprofloxacin 0.3% drops, 5 drops in the ear two times a day for 14 days.
Teach the mother the toileting and drop technique; never use cotton buds and never plug the ear with cotton wool.
Review in 5 days, then every 2 weeks until the ear is dry.
Come back sooner if the child has fever, ear pain, swelling behind the ear, or any danger sign.

[guideline: DIARRHOEA p36] HOME MANAGEMENT - Give the child more fluids more often. Any locally available home fluid should be used e.g: thin soups from boiled vegetables (rice water, sweet potato water, banana water), green coconut water or cooled boiled water - Give child as much fluid as they will drink and after every watery stool - Continue giving the extra fluids until the diarrhoea stops - Give the child plenty of food to prevent undernutrition - Continue to breast feed frequently. - Give fresh fruit or mashed banana to provide potassium. - Give freshly prepared foods. Rice, sweet potato or taro mixed with vegetable and meat or fish are good. Cook and mash or grind food well - Encourage the child to eat; offer food at least 6 times a day - After the diarrhoea stops, give an extra meal each day for two weeks - Ask the mother to bring the child back for review if - Many watery stools or repeated vomitting - Very thirsty or inadequately drinking or eating - Fever and unwell - Blood in the stool - Symptom's persist greater than 2 weeks - Counsel family that due to inflammation of the gut, loose bowel motions may continue for up to 2 weeks however the diarrhoea should slowly improve. - If persistant, see prolonged diarrhoea (>14 days)

They are at risk of becoming cold (hypothermia), having low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia) and infection. Some babies are small because they are born prematurely (before they are due). Infection is an important cause of premature labour. MANAGEMENT - Keep the baby warm - Small babies get cold easily. o Keep the baby skin to skin when possible (together with mother or father) well wrapped up in a warm room. - Start feeds within 1 hour of delivery o Babies who can suck should be breastfed. o Babies who cannot be breastfed should be given expressed breast milk (EBM) by cup and spoon. Change to breastfeeding when the baby starts to suck well from the breast. o Use a NG tube for those less than 1.5kg, or not taking EBM well by cup and spoon or are sick. Nasogastric tubes should be changed twice a week. When the baby can suck well, change to breast feeding or cup and spoon o If EBM unavailable consider IV access and fluids, transfer to hospital

[guideline: EARLY ESSENTIAL NEWBORN CARE p64] Newborn deaths are concentrated towards the first three days of life, especially the first 24 hours. The most common causes of neonatal death are: - Preterm birth complications - Birth asphyxia - Neonatal infections - Congenital abnormalities Early Essential Newborn Care (EENC) practices focus on improving the quality of care during labour, delivery and immediately after birth. Most newborns only require simple supportive care during and after delivery. All babies (including if born by caesarean, sick or preterm), benefit from: - Immediate thorough drying - Skin-to-skin contact - Early and exclusive breast-feeding - Cord clamping after pulsations stop (no earlier than 1 minute). BORN BEFORE ARRIVAL (BBA) Some babies are born at home or before being brought to the clinic or hospital. It is important to weigh the baby, as babies less than 2.5kg need special care. These babies may be at added risk of infection. MANAGEMENT FOR ALL BABIES - Leave baby with mother, support breastfeeding and keep skin-to-skin for 90 minutes (if baby is well) before other treatments below - Weigh and examine the baby o If the baby looks unwell or has fast breathing (>60/minute), give oxygen by nasal catheter and commence treatment for infection o If the baby weighs less than 2.5kg, see guideline for low birth weight babies - Vitamin K (phytomenadione) 1mg IM once o Use 1mg/1ml ampoule. Do NOT use 10mg/ml ampoule. - Hepatitis B and BCG vaccines o Best given at or soon after birth - Apply tetracycline eye ointment ...
Write a short message for the mother of a baby born this morning at the clinic, weight 3.5 kg, she is breastfeeding well and there are no danger signs. She goes home today.
assistant:

STM: EARLY ESSENTIAL NEWBORN CARE
---
Keep the baby skin-to-skin on your chest and breastfeed often, day and night, only breast milk. Keep the cord dry and clean, cover it with a cloth, do not put anything on it. Come back at once if the baby is cold, breathing fast, not feeding, or the cord smells bad. Bring the baby to the clinic in 3 days for a check and vaccines.

[guideline: ASTHMA p21] MANAGEMENT There are two aspects to the management of asthma: i. Treatment of an acute asthma attack ii. Maintenance therapy for frequent & chronic asthma A: TREATMENT OF ACUTE ASTHMA ATTACK Most symptoms of asthma are improved with the use of salbutamol, which causes relaxation of airway muscle spasm. Salbutamol is best given by puffer and spacer: - Dose of Salbutamol using a 100mcg puffer and spacer - Less than 5 years: 6 puffs - More than 5 years: 12 puffs - A spacer can be easily made by cutting a hole at the base of a drinking bottle - Salbutamol can be given by nebuliser in more severe attacks where there is difficulty co-ordinate inhalation with a puffer. Using a 5mg/ml solution - give 2.5mg (0.5ml) in <5yr old and 5mg (1 ml) >5yr old. Dilute to 4ml with normal saline. - Salbutamol tablets (0.15mg/kg, max 4mg) can be used though are not as effective. They should only be used when inhalers are not available

[guideline: OEDEMA p76] Oedema is swelling caused by fluid in the subcutaneous tissues. May be localised to an area (e.g: around the eyes) or generalised (whole body). Can be pitting or non-pitting. The most common causes of neonatal death are: - Preterm birth complications - Birth asphyxia - Neonatal infections - Congenital abnormalities Early Essential Newborn Care (EENC) practices focus on improving the quality of care during labour, delivery and immediately after birth. Most newborns only require simple supportive care during and after delivery. All babies (including if born by caesarean, sick or preterm), benefit from: - Immediate thorough drying - Skin-to-skin contact - Early and exclusive breast-feeding - Cord clamping after pulsations stop (no earlier than 1 minute). BORN BEFORE ARRIVAL (BBA) Some babies are born at home or before being brought to the clinic or hospital. It is important to weigh the baby, as babies less than 2.5kg need special care. These babies may be at added risk of infection. MANAGEMENT FOR ALL BABIES - Leave baby with mother, support breastfeeding and keep skin-to-skin for 90 minutes (if baby is well) before other treatments below - Weigh and examine the baby o If the baby looks unwell or has fast breathing (>60/minute), give oxygen by nasal catheter and commence treatment for infection o If the baby weighs less than 2.5kg, see guideline for low birth weight babies - Vitamin K (phytomenadione) 1mg IM once o Use 1mg/1ml ampoule. Do NOT use 10mg/ml ampoule. - Hepatitis B and BCG vaccines o Best given at or soon after birth - Apply tetracycline eye ointment ...
Baby born just now at the clinic, about 2.5 kg, crying well. Mama is fine. We have no malaria test and no ACT here, and the boat only comes next week. What do I do for the baby in the first hour?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: EARLY ESSENTIAL NEWBORN CARE
---
Dry the baby thoroughly straight away and put baby skin-to-skin on mother's chest, cover both.
Start breastfeeding within the first hour, exclusive, and keep skin-to-skin 90 minutes if baby is well.
Clamp the cord only after pulsations stop, no earlier than 1 minute.
Give vitamin K 1 mg IM once (use the 1 mg/1 ml ampoule, not 10 mg/ml).
Weigh and examine: this baby is 2.5 kg, so see the low birth weight guideline as well.
Give hepatitis B and BCG vaccines and tetracycline eye ointment, and watch breathing (>60/min), feeding, and warmth.

assistant:

This is a burn to the face, neck and hand: refer now in the truck.
Start IV fluids before you go: normal maintenance 54 ml/hr plus extra 4 ml/kg for each 1% burnt. Count the burnt area first.
For 15.9 kg, maintenance is about 50 ml/hr. If the burn is 10%, extra is 4 x 10 x 15.9 = 636 ml, half in first 8 hours = about 40 ml/hr.
Total first 8 hours about 90 ml/hr.
Keep the airway open, do not put ointment on the face, cover with clean cloth.
Write in the referral note: age, weight, percent burnt, fluids started and rate, time.

[guideline: MALARIA p53] INVESTIGATION - Malaria slide (MPS) OR Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) - Blood glucose MANAGEMENT - Consider malaria in any child with a fever. Check MPS or RDT - Note the type of malaria (thin film) and the parasite count (thick film) - A single negative film or antigen does not exclude malaria - If strong suspicion, thick and thin films should be repeated with fever spikes until positive test or 3 negatives obtained - RDT can remain positive for up to 6 weeks after malaria has been treated - Always think about other infections, even if the MPS or RDT is positive - A child with fever and decreased conciousness might have meningitis - Classify as uncomplicated versus complicated and manage accordingly If you cannot test for malaria, treat presumptively Very sick children should be treated for severe malaria

Check MPS or RDT - Note the type of malaria (thin film) and the parasite count (thick film) - A single negative film or antigen does not exclude malaria - If strong suspicion, thick and thin films should be repeated with fever spikes until positive test or 3 negatives obtained - RDT can remain positive for up to 6 weeks after malaria has been treated - Always think about other infections, even if the MPS or RDT is positive - A child with fever and decreased conciousness might have meningitis - Classify as uncomplicated versus complicated and manage accordingly If you cannot test for malaria, treat presumptively Very sick children should be treated for severe malaria

[guideline: NEWBORN BABIES LESS THAN 2.5 KG WEIGHT p66] Babies with low birth weight need special care. They are at risk of becoming cold (hypothermia), having low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia) and infection. Some babies are small because they are born prematurely (before they are due). Infection is an important cause of premature labour. MANAGEMENT - Keep the baby warm - Small babies get cold easily. o Keep the baby skin to skin when possible (together with mother or father) well wrapped up in a warm room. - Start feeds within 1 hour of delivery o Babies who can suck should be breastfed. o Babies who cannot be breastfed should be given expressed breast milk (EBM) by cup and spoon. Change to breastfeeding when the baby starts to suck well from the breast. o Use a NG tube for those less than 1.5kg, or not taking EBM well by cup and spoon or are sick. Nasogastric tubes should be changed twice a week. When the baby can suck well, change to breast feeding or cup and spoon o If EBM unavailable consider IV access and fluids, transfer to hospital

assistant:

Convulsions are a danger sign, not a simple cold. Send this baby to hospital now.
Call the AHC or hospital by radio or phone right away to say a convulsing baby is coming.
Before she leaves: check blood sugar if you can, keep her on her side, do not put anything in her mouth.

Keep her warm, mother stays with her, watch her airway on the way.
Write referral note: age 10 months, weight 9.6 kg, runny nose and cough 1 day, convulsions this morning, RDT result, time of fit, any medicine given.

section: NEWBORN BABIES LESS THAN 2.5 KG WEIGHT
user:
[lang=pis] [rdt=unknown] [act=no] [transport=now]
[guideline: NEWBORN BABIES LESS THAN 2.5 KG WEIGHT p66] Babies with low birth weight need special care. They are at risk of becoming cold (hypothermia), having low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia) and infection. Some babies are small because they are born prematurely (before they are due). Infection is an important cause of premature labour. MANAGEMENT - Keep the baby warm - Small babies get cold easily. o Keep the baby skin to skin when possible (together with mother or father) well wrapped up in a warm room. - Start feeds within 1 hour of delivery o Babies who can suck should be breastfed. o Babies who cannot be breastfed should be given expressed breast milk (EBM) by cup and spoon. Change to breastfeeding when the baby starts to suck well from the breast. o Use a NG tube for those less than 1.5kg, or not taking EBM well by cup and spoon or are sick. Nasogastric tubes should be changed twice a week. When the baby can suck well, change to breast feeding or cup and spoon o If EBM unavailable consider IV access and fluids, transfer to hospital
Bebi blong mi hem 1 month nomoa, weight blong hem 2.3 kg. Hem no saen blong denja, hem dring gud an skin blong hem warm. Wanem nao mi mas duim long klinik?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: NEWBORN BABIES LESS THAN 2.5 KG WEIGHT
---
Bebi 2.3 kg hem smol tumas, mas keepem hem warm oltaem.
Putum hem skin to skin wetem mama o dadi, wrapem gud, putum long warm room.
Statem susu long 1 aoa afta bon. Sapos hem no save susu gud, givim EBM long cup an spoon.
Sapos hem no tekem EBM gud, putum NG tube. Sapos EBM no stap, givim IV fluids an sendem go hospital.
Lukluk evri dei fo saen blong denja: no fit susu, toraot evri samting, skin kol tumas, slip tumas.
Sapos eniwan kam, sendem long AHC o hospital kwiktaem.

[guideline: EARLY ESSENTIAL NEWBORN CARE p64] Newborn deaths are concentrated towards the first three days of life, especially the first 24 hours. The most common causes of neonatal death are: - Preterm birth complications - Birth asphyxia - Neonatal infections - Congenital abnormalities Early Essential Newborn Care (EENC) practices focus on improving the quality of care during labour, delivery and immediately after birth. Most newborns only require simple supportive care during and after delivery. All babies (including if born by caesarean, sick or preterm), benefit from: - Immediate thorough drying - Skin-to-skin contact - Early and exclusive breast-feeding - Cord clamping after pulsations stop (no earlier than 1 minute). BORN BEFORE ARRIVAL (BBA) Some babies are born at home or before being brought to the clinic or hospital. It is important to weigh the baby, as babies less than 2.5kg need special care. These babies may be at added risk of infection. MANAGEMENT FOR ALL BABIES - Leave baby with mother, support breastfeeding and keep skin-to-skin for 90 minutes (if baby is well) before other treatments below - Weigh and examine the baby o If the baby looks unwell or has fast breathing (>60/minute), give oxygen by nasal catheter and commence treatment for infection o If the baby weighs less than 2.5kg, see guideline for low birth weight babies - Vitamin K (phytomenadione) 1mg IM once o Use 1mg/1ml ampoule. Do NOT use 10mg/ml ampoule. - Hepatitis B and BCG vaccines o Best given at or soon after birth - Apply tetracycline eye ointment ...
Baby born at home last night, brought in this morning. Mother says baby is about 1 month old and weighs around 1.8 kg on our scale. Baby is feeding a little but feels cold and is breathing about 70 times a minute. What should I do?
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NOW
STM: EARLY ESSENTIAL NEWBORN CARE
---
Fast breathing over 60 a minute in a small baby is a danger sign. Send this baby to hospital now, transport is available.
Keep baby skin-to-skin with mother, dry and warm, and cover the head.
Support breastfeeding and let baby feed if able.
Give vitamin K 1 mg IM once using the 1 mg/1 ml ampoule, not the 10 mg/ml.
Give oxygen by nasal catheter if you have it while waiting for transport.
Tell the hospital the weight 1.8 kg and breathing rate.

[guideline: BREAST FEEDING p26] PROMOTE BREAST FEEDING - It is safe, simple, readily available and cheap - It contains all the nutrients that the baby needs to grow - It reduces the risk of diarrhoea, pneumonia, malnutrition and other diseases - Helps encourage bonding between mother and baby FACTS ABOUT BREAST FEEDING - Breast feeding should begin within the first hour after delivery - The first yellow milk a mother makes (colostrum) should be given to the baby. o It should not be thrown away as it contains important immunoglobulins that are part of the baby's defense against infection - The easiest and best schedule is 'on-demand' breast feeding o Infants who cannot demand feed (such as low birth weight or sick babies) should be fed every 2-3 hours o Infants who cannot suck on the breast (eg. very premature babies) should be given expressed breast milk (EBM) by cup/spoon or by NG tube - Ideally all babies should be exclusively breast fed for the first 6 months o Solids should be introduced from 6 months o Cow's milk or powdered milk should be avoided before the age of 12 months because of the risk of iron-deficiency anaemia - Breast feeding should continue for as long as possible. - Breast feeding policies should be supported and upheld always - Bottles with teats and baby cups with spouts should discouraged. o They are difficult to sterilize and may result in infections such as diarrhoea - For facts about breast feeding in HIV positive mothers

Do not give any other medicines or feeds that are not in the manual.
Write the referral note: age 54 months, weight 16.9 kg, oedema both feet, poor weight gain 3 months, breastfeeding stopped.
Tell mama to go with the child and bring any clinic cards.

[guideline: COLDS/ URTI p31] - Colds or URTI (Upper Respiratory Tract Infections) are a common cause of fever and cough in children - Mostly are viral and therefore do not usually require antibiotic treament SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - Fever - Runny nose, sneezing - Cough - NO "danger signs": NOT fast breathing, NO chest indrawing, NO stridor CAUSES - Common colds are caused by viral infections INVESTIGATIONS - Consider malaria slide MANAGEMENT - Examine the child carefully - If no fever present, reassure the parents and explain why the child is coughing - Explain that coughing helps to get rid of secretions in the chest and throat - It is not uncommon to have persistant coughing for up to a month (post viral cough) - If "no danger signs" or other causes of chronic cough (e.g: TB), it is ok to reassure the parents and arrange follow up - If fever present - Check ears and treat otitis media if present - Check throat, if pus/white exudate and tender enlarged lymph nodes, on tonsils give: - Benzathine penicillin IM single dose - Child weighs < 20kg give 450mg (0.6 mega units) - Child weighs > 20kg give 900mg (1.2 mega units) OR - Penicillin V - Child < 10 years give 250mg orally every 12 hours for 10 days - Child > 10 years give 500mg orally every 12 hours for 10 days - Consider antimalarials - Give paracetamol if in pain - Encourage oral fluids if ...
6 months baby, 7.1 kg, little bit cough and nose running 2 days, still taking breast good, no fever now. I checked chest, no indrawing, breathing normal. We have RDT ready. Transport truck is here now. Do I need to send?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: COLDS/ URTI
---
No need to send, this baby has no danger signs. Do the malaria RDT since you have it; if positive, treat per malaria protocol. Check ears for otitis media and throat for pus on tonsils with tender nodes; if present, give benzathine penicillin 450 mg IM single dose (under 20 kg). If all clear, no antibiotics. Give paracetamol 15 mg/kg, about 110 mg, if uncomfortable. Encourage mum to keep breastfeeding often. Tell her to come back fast if baby gets fast breathing, chest indrawing, stops feeding, or gets very hot again.

The RDT came back positive this morning for a 2 month old boy, around 3.8 kg. He is feeding and no danger signs but we have no artemether-lumefantrine left in the clinic and no boat until Friday. What can I do?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: MALARIA
---
RDT positive, so treat as malaria; this baby is under 2 months so use the young infant drug doses.
No artemether-lumefantrine: give second line quinine sulphate 10 mg/kg, that is 38 mg, by mouth every 8 hours as the manual directs.
Keep offering breast milk and give paracetamol 15 mg/kg (about 57 mg) every 6 hours if the skin is hot.
Check every day for danger signs: convulsions, not able to drink or breastfeed, vomits everything, lethargic, fast breathing, stiff neck, pallor.
If any danger sign appears, call the AHC by radio and refer now, do not wait for the boat.

This 6-month baby girl, around 5.4 kg, came in very drowsy. Her mother says she has not breastfed since last night. She is sweaty and her hands are shaking a little. We have RDT strips here but no transport today, the boat broke down. What should I do first?
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NOW
STM: HYPOGLYCAEMIA

Drowsy and not feeding are danger signs. This is likely hypoglycaemia.
Check blood sugar now with CBG. If less than 2.5 mmol/L, give sugar immediately.
If dextrose available: give IV dextrose 10% 5.4 ml (1 ml/kg). If no IV, put sugar water on gums and under tongue.
Give breastmilk or sugar water by cup or spoon if she can swallow. Keep her warm.
Call AHC or hospital by radio now. This baby needs urgent transfer when boat is fixed.
