[guideline: NEWBORN BABIES - NEONATAL INFECTIONS p69] NEONATAL MENINGITIS Meningitis should be considered in all infants presenting with non-specific signs of sepsis, as the classical signs of meningitis are often absent. Babies who are very unwell may have meningitis and should be referred to hospital. Additional features can include: - Very drowsy or irritable with high pitched cry - Reduced feeding - Apnoea's - Bulging fontanelle - Fitting Babies with suspected meningitis should have a lumbar puncture - If the CSF is cloudy, blood stained, or you cannot obtain CSF and you think the baby has meningitis, treat for meningitis
Baby is 6 days old, weight 2.9 kg. Since last night she is not feeding well and she feels hot. She is not drowsy, no fitting. The next boat is tomorrow morning and we have no malaria test kit. What should I do?
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NEXT_TRANSPORT
STM: NEWBORN BABIES - NEONATAL INFECTIONS
---
This baby is under 2 months with fever, so treat as sepsis and refer to hospital. Keep her warm and feed her by cup or NG tube if she will not suck.
Start ampicillin and gentamicin now while you wait for the boat.
Give ampicillin 150 mg IV/IM (50 mg/kg) and gentamicin 15 mg (5 mg/kg) once daily.
Watch for drowsy, high-pitched cry, not feeding, apnoea, bulging fontanelle or fitting. If any come, call the AHC by radio and send her sooner.
Write the note: age, weight, feeds, temperature, drugs and times.

[guideline: MEASLES p61] - Measles is a viral infection which causes a red, raised rash - It is transmitted by droplets produced by sneezing and coughing - The incubation period is between 7 and 21 days - Measles is very infectious from 7 days before until 2 days after the rash appears SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - Fever (before the rash appears) - Blotchy red rash, starting on head/neck moving down over the body (day 3-7) - Look for the 3 C's: Cough, Coryza (runny nose), Conjunctivitis - Sore mouth - Koplick spots (may have small white spots in mouth) - Diarrhoea PREVENTION - Immunisation - Avoiding contact with others who are infected MANAGEMENT Admission/OutpatientsMost can be managed as Outpatients Admit if complications: pneumonia, diarrhoea, dehydration, stridor Admit children with underlying cardiac disease/respiratory disease Admit if immunocompromised Malnutrition Consider nutritional status and SAM management Treat co-existing infection Oral thrush, conjunctivitis, pneumonia or diarrhoea Refer to relevant section in STM for treatment advice Consider malaria Consider investigation and treatment if from high risk area Give Vitamin A <6 months: 50,000 Units, 6 months - 1 year: 100,000 Units, >1 year: 200,000 Units Daily for 2 days. Give 3rd dose 2-4 weeks later if eye signs suggestive of Vit A deficiency Immunise contacts Give measles vaccine to all siblings aged 6 months-5 years if not fully vaccinated If unclear vaccination history ...

[guideline: MALARIA p53] INVESTIGATION - Malaria slide (MPS) OR Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) - Blood glucose MANAGEMENT - Consider malaria in any child with a fever. Check MPS or RDT - Note the type of malaria (thin film) and the parasite count (thick film) - A single negative film or antigen does not exclude malaria - If strong suspicion, thick and thin films should be repeated with fever spikes until positive test or 3 negatives obtained - RDT can remain positive for up to 6 weeks after malaria has been treated - Always think about other infections, even if the MPS or RDT is positive - A child with fever and decreased conciousness might have meningitis - Classify as uncomplicated versus complicated and manage accordingly If you cannot test for malaria, treat presumptively Very sick children should be treated for severe malaria
Baby 4 months, around 6 kg. Mother says he had fever since yesterday, now he is very sleepy and hard to wake, and his body looks yellow. The boat to town leaves tomorrow morning, no other transport.
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NEXT_TRANSPORT
STM: MALARIA
---
This is severe malaria: jaundice and lethargy are danger signs. Baby must go to hospital on tomorrow's boat.
While you wait: treat for severe malaria. Give artesunate 14.4 mg (2.4 mg per kg) IM now, repeat at 12 hours, then daily. If no artesunate IM, put artesunate 60 mg rectally (10 mg per kg).
Check blood sugar if you can. Give breast milk or sugar water if baby can suck.
Keep baby warm. If convulsions start, turn on side, clear mouth, do not put anything inside.
Radio the AHC now: say jaundiced lethargic 4-month baby, RDT not done, artesunate given with times. Write referral note: age, weight, jaundice, lethargy, fever, all drug doses and times.

6-year-old boy, 19.9 kg, from the village clinic. Doctor wants me to give phenytoin loading dose for a seizure but I need to prepare the IV. How much do I draw up and how do I dilute it? We have the 250 mg ampoules here.
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: PAEDIATRIC DRUG DOSES
---
Phenytoin loading dose is 15-20 mg/kg for a child with seizures.
For 19.9 kg: use 300 mg (15 mg/kg) to 398 mg (20 mg/kg), rounded to practical measurement.
Draw up the 250 mg/5 mL ampoule: 6 mL gives 300 mg, or 8 mL gives 400 mg.
Dilute with NS to 5 mg/mL for infusion, or give slow IV push 1-2 mg/kg/minute, maximum 50 mg/minute.
Flush well with NS after, and inspect for particles or haze before use.

Boy 5 years, around 18 kg. He started fitting in the clinic just now, this fit is going past 5 minutes. No midazolam on my shelf, I have diazepam. What do I do?
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NOW
STM: CONVULSIONS
---
A fit lasting over 5-10 minutes is an emergency: secure airway, place him on his side, suction if you can, give oxygen, and check blood sugar.
If the fit is still going: diazepam IV 3.6 mg (0.2 mg/kg, max 10 mg) or PR 5.4 mg (0.3 mg/kg, max 10 mg).
Keep bag and mask ready and make sure he is breathing after each dose.
He needs hospital now - call the AHC or hospital by radio or phone for the transfer and keep him on his side while you wait.
Check blood sugar and treat as per the hypoglycaemia guideline.

Child 2 and a half years, 12.6 kg, has fever and rash spreading down the body for 2 days, plus cough, runny nose and sore red eyes. Eating and drinking okay, no vomiting, no fit. We do not know if we have RDT, and no ACT on the shelf. Next boat is in two days. What is the treatment?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: MEASLES
---
Measles is the working diagnosis: fever, blotchy rash from head down, cough, runny nose and red eyes.
No red flag, so outpatient care is fine until the boat.
Give Vitamin A 200,000 Units today and again tomorrow (over 1 year).
Give paracetamol 190 mg (15 mg per kg) every 6 hours if hot.
Check for pneumonia, diarrhoea, dehydration and mouth thrush, and treat per STM.
Before the boat, look for fast breathing, chest indrawing, stridor, or stopping drinking; if any, send now and call the AHC by radio.

user:
[lang=pis] [rdt=yes] [act=no] [transport=next_boat]
[guideline: NEWBORN BABIES LESS THAN 2.5 KG WEIGHT p66] Babies with low birth weight need special care. They are at risk of becoming cold (hypothermia), having low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia) and infection. Some babies are small because they are born prematurely (before they are due). Infection is an important cause of premature labour. MANAGEMENT - Keep the baby warm - Small babies get cold easily. o Keep the baby skin to skin when possible (together with mother or father) well wrapped up in a warm room. - Start feeds within 1 hour of delivery o Babies who can suck should be breastfed. o Babies who cannot be breastfed should be given expressed breast milk (EBM) by cup and spoon. Change to breastfeeding when the baby starts to suck well from the breast. o Use a NG tube for those less than 1.5kg, or not taking EBM well by cup and spoon or are sick. Nasogastric tubes should be changed twice a week. When the baby can suck well, change to breast feeding or cup and spoon o If EBM unavailable consider IV access and fluids, transfer to hospital

This is severe malaria with convulsion and lethargy: danger signs. Send her to hospital now in the truck.
Before she leaves, check blood sugar if you can. If BSL is low, give IV dextrose or oral sugar water if she can swallow safely.
Give the first dose of artesunate 43 mg IM (2.4 mg/kg) now if you have it, or start quinine if that is what the clinic stocks.
Keep her on her side during the journey, monitor breathing, and do not give too much fluid.
Call the hospital by radio or phone to warn them she is coming with cerebral malaria.
Write the referral note: age, weight, RDT positive, time and description of fit, BSL result, drugs and times given.

[guideline: NEWBORN BABIES LESS THAN 2.5 KG WEIGHT p66] Babies with low birth weight need special care. They are at risk of becoming cold (hypothermia), having low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia) and infection. Some babies are small because they are born prematurely (before they are due). Infection is an important cause of premature labour. MANAGEMENT - Keep the baby warm - Small babies get cold easily. o Keep the baby skin to skin when possible (together with mother or father) well wrapped up in a warm room. - Start feeds within 1 hour of delivery o Babies who can suck should be breastfed. o Babies who cannot be breastfed should be given expressed breast milk (EBM) by cup and spoon. Change to breastfeeding when the baby starts to suck well from the breast. o Use a NG tube for those less than 1.5kg, or not taking EBM well by cup and spoon or are sick. Nasogastric tubes should be changed twice a week. When the baby can suck well, change to breast feeding or cup and spoon o If EBM unavailable consider IV access and fluids, transfer to hospital

Fever over 7 days needs careful checking for abscess, typhoid, TB or rheumatic fever.
Give paracetamol 112 mg every 4 to 6 hours if irritable (15 mg/kg, max 4 doses in 24 hours).
Look for hidden abscess, do urine dipstick if possible, and check joints for swelling or pain.

Come back tomorrow or sooner if fever still high; the cause must be found.

[guideline: SKIN DISEASES p96] Skin disease is common in children in the Solomon Islands and can be caused by bacteria, fungus (e.g. ringworm), parasites (e.g. scabies) or viruses (e.g. molluscum contagiosum). They can also lead to serious infections of the blood. Also consider non-infectious causes of skin disease (e.g. eczema, allergies). PREVENTION OF SKIN DISEASES Skin diseases can often be prevented by good skin hygiene and use of soap and water Advise parents - Keep skin clean. Wash with soap and water daily, drying well between fingers and toes - Do not share towels between infected children - Get treatment for small skin sores early before they get big - Use of medicated soaps may prevent small skin sores becoming serious Prevention of spreading infection and re-infection - Many skin diseases are contagious. Always treat other infected family members or contacts at the same time.

---
These look like infected sores (impetigo). Wash the sores with soap and water, dry well, and tell the mother to keep the skin clean daily.
Give cloxacillin by mouth if the sores are extensive: 25 mg per kg four times a day, so about 800 mg for 31.8 kg.
Do not share towels, and treat any other family member who has sores at the same time.
Come back in 2 days if the sores are spreading, the child gets a fever, or the leg becomes swollen and painful.

A father hit his 3 month old baby and left a mark on the back. The mother wants to know if she should report him to police and who gets custody of the baby. What should I tell her?
assistant:
ACTION: ASK_PERSON
STM: NONE
---
I am not sure about police reports and custody. That is not in my manual, it is a legal and protection matter.
Contact the nurse in charge and the doctor at the AHC or NRH today, and also the welfare or child protection officer for your province.
Tell them: 3 month old baby, mark on the back from a hit, who is at home, and where the family lives.
Check the baby now for any other injury, and if the baby is not feeding, is very sleepy, or has a fit, refer now.
Keep the baby with the mother and do not send the family away before someone senior has spoken to them.

Ask the nurse in charge or phone the doctor at the AHC or NRH about yellow fever and typhoid vaccines for travel.
Tell them: child is 2 years old, family is travelling to Australia next month, and what vaccines the child has already had.

Please just tell me the name of the sickness. The baby is 10 months and has been hot and crying since yesterday. I want to write the diagnosis in the book before the boat comes.
assistant:
ACTION: ASK_PERSON
STM: NONE
---
I cannot give a diagnosis without seeing the baby. Only the doctor or nurse in charge can name the sickness.
Phone the AHC or NRH and say: 10 months old, hot and crying since yesterday, and what you can see.
Write in the book what you observe, not a disease name: temperature, feeding, breathing, any rash.
Look now for danger signs: not drinking, vomiting everything, fits, sleepy, chest indrawing, stiff neck.
If any of those are there, send the baby with the next boat and radio ahead that the baby is coming.

[guideline: NEWBORN BABIES - NEONATAL INFECTIONS p69] NEONATAL MENINGITIS Meningitis should be considered in all infants presenting with non-specific signs of sepsis, as the classical signs of meningitis are often absent. Babies who are very unwell may have meningitis and should be referred to hospital. Additional features can include: - Very drowsy or irritable with high pitched cry - Reduced feeding - Apnoea's - Bulging fontanelle - Fitting Babies with suspected meningitis should have a lumbar puncture - If the CSF is cloudy, blood stained, or you cannot obtain CSF and you think the baby has meningitis, treat for meningitis

SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - Exremely itchy rash mainly between fingers, wrists, in the axilla, around the naval, genitals and inner sides of feet. - Infants have a more widespread distribution of rash - Itching may be much worse at night - Scratching may cause secondary bacterial infection

[guideline: ANAEMIA p18] Treatment of anaemia - Consider malaria treatment and give hookworm treatment with albendazole - Give advice on good nutrition o Diet rich in meat, fish, chicken, peanuts, green leafy vegetables, beans, lentils o Eating raw, washed vegetables and fruit (such as paw-paw, mango, pineapple and orange) helps the body to absorb iron - Give iron treatment (calculate doses carefully as Iron is toxic on overdose) o Re-check Hb after 4 weeks o Should be given orally if possible - Dose: 2 - 6 mg/kg/day elemental iron (max 200mg) - There are different formulations available for iron. Always calculate on the amount of elemental iron in the mixture For Ferrous mixture 20mg/1ml (contains 6mg of elemental iron in 1ml): WEIGHT (kg) MIXTURE 3 - 5.9 6 - 9.9 10 - 14.9 15 - 19.9 20mg/ml 1ml 2.5ml 4ml 5ml - Plan to continue oral iron replacement for 3 months, recheck Hb o If no improvement, firstly check compliance with medication o Consider increasing dose o Consider alternative diagnosis (e.g chronic infection or disease) - If the child cannot take oral iron, consider IM injection. Discuss with paediatrician.
